title: The Keys to Hitting a Target
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Using a family tradition of riflery and archery at summer camp, Stuart builds an extended analogy between marksmanship and student goal-setting: it's far easier to hit a target you can see clearly than one obscured by fog, just as it's easier to work toward a specific goal than a vague one. He contrasts vague student goals ("improve my grades," "do better in science") with concrete rewrites of the same goals, arguing that vagueness is what causes motivation to deteriorate over time. Drawing the marksmanship analogy further, he notes that expert shooters focus on discrete, controllable actions and observe results to adjust -- the same discipline he wants students to apply to schoolwork. The piece ends with two practical takeaways: maintain a clearly articulated class purpose ("Everest Statement") and periodically walk students through structured goal-setting exercises like WOOP.
points: Central analogy: aiming at a goal obscured by "the fog of vagueness" is functionally like shooting a target in thick fog -- clarity, not effort, is the limiting factor.
Stuart gives paired examples (vague goal vs. specific rewrite) for grades, focus, and science performance, giving teachers a concrete template for helping students reword their own goals.
He explicitly names vague goals as producing "spotty, mood-dependent effort and frustration," linking the abstract clarity argument to a specific motivational failure mode.
Two actionable takeaways close the piece: maintain a clear, regularly repeated class purpose statement, and periodically run structured goal-setting protocols like WOOP.
quotes: Which do you think is easier: shooting at a target on a clear day or shooting at a target in thick fog? Definitely a clear day. In the same way, I tell them it's much easier to aim at a goal that is clear versus a goal that is obscured by the fog of vagueness.
Improving my grades is a pretty vague goal. Getting all six of my classes up to a D- or better is a much clearer one.
When success is vague in our classrooms or in our students' minds — and I'd argue in many classes, both of those things are often commonplace — motivation is bound to deteriorate.
It is hard to care about a vague goal — especially over the long term. Vague goals lead to spotty, mood-dependent effort and frustration in the end.
Make sure you have a very clear (and regularly articulated) Everest Statement — this is what our class is all about. Periodically guide your students through goal-setting exercises (such as WOOP).
